records.place: Modena, with its Sorbara vineyard at Sozzigalli to the north, Emilia

wine.name: Vecchia Modena Premium
wine.grapes: Lambrusco di Sorbara alone, though the DOC would allow Salamino for up to two fifths of the wine.
wine.sites: The Sozzigalli vineyard on the left bank of the Secchia, north of Modena, on clay and silt laid down by centuries of floods, where the house keeps old Sorbara clones.
wine.making: Sorbara alone is given a light maceration on its skins, then the must is drawn off and chilled. Its sparkle comes from a slow fermentation in a sealed pressure tank, the cuve close or Charmat way, which traps the gas; the wine is bottled clear, with no sediment.
wine.glass: Pale ruby to deep pink under a pink froth; violet, wild strawberry and sour cherry over sharp, mouth watering acidity, light in body and bone dry, with almost no tannin.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a year or two of the harvest, while its scent of violets and its froth are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass or a tulip shows its scent better than a narrow flute.

label.means: The DOC of the Sorbara zone north of Modena: at least 60 per cent Sorbara, here Sorbara alone.
Old Modena: a name of the house's from its first century, brought back in 1980 for a dry Sorbara.
The honourable mention the house's Lambrusco won in Paris in 1900, which later labels recall.

records.table: Vecchia Modena Premium is Cleto Chiarli's Lambrusco di Sorbara: pale pink, bone dry and sharp, made from Sorbara alone grown at Sozzigalli north of Modena and given its froth in a sealed tank. Pour it cold beside prosciutto, mortadella and Parmigiano Reggiano.
records.story: The house's founder kept an inn in the old centre of Modena, the Osteria dell'Artigliere as the house names it, and poured there the Lambrusco made in its cellar. In 1860, by the house's account, he gave up the inn to make Lambrusco alone, refermented in its bottle as the wine was then made, and the house dates its founding from that year. At the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1900 its Lambrusco won a Mention Honorable, an early mark of the wine abroad. The name Vecchia Modena, old Modena, dates from that first century: the house took it off its list in the middle of the twentieth century and brought it back in 1980 as a dry Sorbara, presented at the national congress of Italy's oenologists. In 2000, by the house's account, the family's estate branch, which carries the founder's name, began its own wines with the Premium, a Sorbara chosen from the Sozzigalli vineyard on the left bank of the Secchia. Later labels add the words Mention Honorable. For a sommelier the Premium is a lesson in dry Sorbara: pale, sharp and scented, the opposite pole to dark Grasparossa, and the bottle that shows a guest Lambrusco need not be sweet.

others.name: Lambrusco di Sorbara del Fondatore
others.note: Sorbara refermented in its own bottle, the old way of the founder's day, as its name recalls.

others.name: Lambrusco Grasparossa di Castelvetro
others.note: Darker and more tannic, from the foothills south of Modena: the other face of the family.

traps: Vecchia Modena Premium is Sorbara alone, though the Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC lets Salamino make up to 40 per cent of the wine.
The Premium takes its sparkle in a sealed tank and pours clear; the house's Lambrusco di Sorbara del Fondatore is the one refermented in bottle.
Pale as it pours, Vecchia Modena Premium is a red Lambrusco di Sorbara, not a rosé: Sorbara is the pale member of the Lambrusco family.

cards.front: Cleto Chiarli Vecchia Modena Premium: which grape, and from which vineyard?
cards.back: Lambrusco di Sorbara alone, from the Sozzigalli vineyard on the left bank of the Secchia, north of Modena.

cards.front: What did Chiarli's Lambrusco win at the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1900?
cards.back: A Mention Honorable, which later labels of Vecchia Modena Premium name.

questions.q: A guest asks how Cleto Chiarli's Vecchia Modena Premium gets its froth. Which answer is right?
opts: A slow fermentation in a sealed pressure tank
A second fermentation in its own bottle
Carbon dioxide added just before bottling
The traditional method, riddled and disgorged
questions.exp: The Premium ferments slowly in cuve close, a sealed tank that traps its sparkle, and pours clear; the house keeps refermentation in bottle for its Lambrusco del Fondatore.

questions.q: Cleto Chiarli took the name Vecchia Modena off its list in the middle of the twentieth century. When did it bring it back as a dry Sorbara?
questions.exp: The name returned in 1980, presented at the national congress of Italy's oenologists; 1900 is the Paris honourable mention and 2000 the year the estate branch began with the Premium.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35; the house's own pages (chiarli.it) were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: the label reads Vecchia Modena Premium, later ones adding Mention Honorable, Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC, and the wine is made in cuve close, a sealed tank, not refermented in bottle; the house's sheet says a pris de mousse of the must alone.

The dates of 1860, the Paris mention of 1900, the relaunch of 1980 and the first Premium of 2000 rest on the house's own pages, hedged as its account; the Paris mention is also on a merchant's page, and the house's sustainability report gives the Osteria dell'Artigliere.

Left out on one source or as a claim of a first: the mushroom shaped cork the house says the founder brought in, the English bottle of 1900, the cellar lost to bombing in the Second World War, the first Lambrusco to win a guide's top award (a rating in any case), the four months in steel and the founder's dates, so the founder is described and not named apart from the house's name.

Region record in tension, slightly: it puts Sorbara on lighter, sandier alluvium, while the house's Sozzigalli page describes clay and silt laid by floods; the record keeps the house's words for its own vineyard.

Living names met, none in the fragment's prose save the house's own name: Anselmo Chiarli and Mauro Chiarli of the fourth generation (a merchant calls them the founders, wrongly), for people.json once a refuter has settled that both are living.

records.place: Gaida, Reggio Emilia, and Montecchio Emilia in the Enza valley, Emilia

wine.name: Concerto
wine.appellation: Reggiano DOC, Lambrusco Reggiano on the label
wine.grapes: Lambrusco Salamino alone, from the family's own Tenuta La Rampata.
wine.sites: Tenuta La Rampata at Montecchio Emilia, in the valley of the Enza in the province of Reggio Emilia: a single estate of Lambrusco Salamino on clay and gravel, which the family studied before planting and judged suited to the variety, its vines on spurred cordon and cropped low.
wine.making: The grapes are fermented in stainless steel, and the wine takes its sparkle in a sealed pressure tank, the Martinotti or Charmat method, before it is bottled young as a dry frizzante, with no oak at any stage.
wine.glass: Deep ruby under a vivid violet froth; sour cherry, wild raspberry and blackberry with a hint of violet, a brisk fizz, light tannin and a dry, clean finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a year or two of the harvest as the house advises, while its fruit and its froth are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass or a tulip rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: The Lambrusco of the Reggiano DOC, drawn from the province of Reggio Emilia.
Dry: the sweetness word that comes before amabile and dolce on a Lambrusco.
Lightly sparkling, at a lower pressure than a spumante.

records.table: Concerto is Medici Ermete's dry Reggiano Lambrusco, Lambrusco Salamino alone from the family's La Rampata estate in the Enza valley. Deep ruby under a violet froth, it tastes of sour cherry and raspberry with a light grip: pour it cold beside salumi, tortellini or lasagne.
records.story: The house dates itself to 1890, when its founder, who already kept three taverns on the Via Emilia, started a winery to make use of the family's vineyards. His son, whose name the house carries, enlarged the business and made its name, and the generation after him began to send the wine abroad. By the end of the 1980s, as the house tells it, the Lambrusco trade of Emilia had collapsed under a glut of lesser wine. The fourth generation answered by replanting the vineyards, changing how the vines were trained and cutting yields well below what the rules allowed, and in 1993 that work gave Concerto: Lambrusco Salamino from one estate, Tenuta La Rampata, made dry at a time when, as the family tells it, a dry Lambrusco was hardly thought of. Beside the sweet Lambrusco that Riunite, the cooperative of Reggio Emilia, had made famous in the United States in the 1970s, Concerto argued that Lambrusco could be the wine of one place. At La Rampata, a nineteenth century house among the vines of the Enza valley, the family also keeps an acetaia for the traditional balsamic vinegar of Reggio Emilia. For a sommelier Concerto is the dry face of Reggiano: Salamino rather than Sorbara, deep ruby where Sorbara is pale, and the bottle to pour when a guest believes every Lambrusco is sweet.

others.name: Granconcerto
others.note: A red brut sparkling wine of Lambrusco Salamino, made by the traditional method, its second fermentation in the bottle.

others.name: I Quercioli Reggiano Lambrusco Secco
others.note: A dry Reggiano Lambrusco of Salamino and Marani, from the house's Quercioli vineyard outside Reggio Emilia.

traps: Concerto is Lambrusco Salamino from the province of Reggio Emilia, not Lambrusco di Sorbara from the plain north of Modena.
Concerto is labelled Reggiano DOC; Lambrusco Salamino di Santa Croce is a different DOC, around Carpi in the province of Modena.
Concerto is secco, dry, though the Reggiano DOC also allows amabile and dolce wines, so read the sweetness word on any Reggiano.

cards.front: Medici Ermete Concerto: which Lambrusco grape, and from which estate?
cards.back: Lambrusco Salamino alone, from the family's Tenuta La Rampata at Montecchio Emilia in the Enza valley.

cards.front: What state was the Lambrusco trade of Emilia in when Medici Ermete made its first Concerto?
cards.back: By the house's account it had collapsed at the end of the 1980s under a glut of lesser wine; the family replanted, cut yields and made Concerto in 1993.

questions.q: A guest who knows only pale Sorbara is poured Medici Ermete's Concerto and asks why it is so deep in colour. Which reason fits?
opts: It is Lambrusco Salamino, a deeply coloured member of the family
It is aged for two years in new oak barrels
It is blended with Sangiovese grown in Romagna
It is refermented in bottle and left on its lees
questions.exp: Concerto is Lambrusco Salamino alone, which gives deep ruby wine; it is made in steel and a pressure tank, with no oak, no Sangiovese and no refermentation in bottle.

questions.q: Medici Ermete dates itself to 1890. What did its founder already run when he started the winery?
opts: Three taverns on the Via Emilia
A balsamic vinegar loft in Modena
A cooperative cellar in Reggio
A wine shop in Bologna
questions.exp: By the house's account he already kept three taverns on the Via Emilia and started the winery to use the family's own vineyards, not a cooperative's grapes.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35, one of them after the first draft; the house's own pages (medici.it) were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: the house dates itself to 1890 (its history page and Itinerari nel Gusto), Concerto is Lambrusco Salamino alone from Tenuta La Rampata, and its first year is 1993 on the house's page and in Gambero Rosso International; its importer once dated the launch to 1994, and the house's thirtieth anniversary of 2024 fits either, so the record says the house's 1993.

Claims of a first left out: the first single vineyard Lambrusco (its importer), the first Lambrusco to win international awards (the house) and the first to take a guide's top award (a rating in any case), since Cleto Chiarli makes a like claim for its Premium.

The Martinotti or Charmat method rests on two merchants (Callmewine, Superiore.de); the house's sheet says fermented in stainless steel tank and its Italian sheet natural fermentation, so the record says no more than the tank.

La Rampata is at Montecchio Emilia in the Enza valley by the house's visits page, a nineteenth century house with the acetaia; Gaida di Reggio Emilia is the house's office and shop, and the merchants who put the vineyard near Gaida are mistaken.
The founder and his son are described, not named, for want of their dates; the house's name carries the son's.

Living names met, none in the fragment's prose: Alberto Medici, Pierluigi Medici and Alessandra Medici of the fourth generation and Alessandro Medici, quoted by Gambero Rosso International, for people.json; the third generation's Valter and Giorgio Medici are not settled.

records.place: Cristo di Sorbara, north of Modena, Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC, Emilia

wine.name: Radice
wine.grapes: Lambrusco di Sorbara alone, from the family's own vines.
wine.sites: The Cristo, the historic heart of the Sorbara zone, on the strip of land between the Secchia and the Panaro rivers, on loose, mostly silty and sandy alluvium.
wine.making: The free run juice and the gently pressed must are made as a white wine is, off the skins. The wine is bottled once, at the start of March, and then referments in that bottle with its own native yeasts. It rests there on its lees and is never disgorged, so it pours a little cloudy.
wine.glass: Pale salmon pink and a little hazy; wild rose, raspberry, white currant and orange peel, bone dry and light, with sharp acidity, a fine froth and a savoury touch from its lees.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, while its froth and its scent of roses are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, or a little warmer as the house suggests; no need to decant, but stand the bottle so the lees settle, or pour them in; a white wine glass.

label.means: Italian for root: the house's Sorbara refermented in its own bottle.
The DOC of the Sorbara zone north of Modena: at least 60 per cent Sorbara, here Sorbara alone.

records.table: Radice is Paltrinieri's Lambrusco di Sorbara from the Cristo, the sandy heart of the Sorbara zone: pale salmon pink, bone dry and sharp, refermented in its own bottle and left on its lees. Pour it cold, a little hazy, beside prosciutto and gnocco fritto.
records.story: The Paltrinieri family dates its bond with Sorbara to 1926, when the founder of the family's cellar began making wine in the Cristo, the historic heart of the zone on the narrow strip of land between the Secchia and the Panaro rivers, north of Modena. The family has run the estate ever since. In 1970 Lambrusco di Sorbara became a DOC of its own, asking at least 60 per cent of the Sorbara grape, a vine that sets fruit poorly and gives pale, sharp and scented wine. Across the zone most Lambrusco came to take its sparkle in pressure tanks; Radice keeps the older way of the countryside, in which the wine finishes its fermentation in the bottle and leaves a cloudy sediment, a way that small growers have brought back. The family makes it from Sorbara alone, pressed as a white wine, bottled once at the start of March and left on its lees. Beside it, Leclisse shows the same grape given a long fermentation in tank. In 2026 the house marked its hundredth year with a day of wine, food and music. For a sommelier Radice is the wine that shows what refermentation in bottle does to Sorbara: hazier and more savoury, as sharp as ever, and true to the root its name recalls.

others.name: Leclisse
others.note: Lambrusco di Sorbara made without maceration and given a long second fermentation in tank: the house's other Sorbara.

others.name: LaRiserva
others.note: A Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC spumante brut, made off the skins and kept some twelve months on its lees in tank.

traps: Radice is refermented in its own bottle and left on its lees, so it is hazy; Leclisse, from the same house, takes its sparkle in tank.
Paltrinieri grows Sorbara in the Cristo on the plain north of Modena; Grasparossa is the hill Lambrusco of Castelvetro, south of the city.
Radice is a dry frizzante, though the Lambrusco di Sorbara DOC also allows amabile and dolce wines.

cards.front: Paltrinieri Radice: how does it get its sparkle?
cards.back: It referments in its own bottle with native yeasts after a single bottling at the start of March, and is left on its lees.

cards.front: In which part of the Sorbara zone are the Paltrinieri family's vines, and since when?
cards.back: In the Cristo, the historic heart of the zone between the Secchia and the Panaro, since 1926.

questions.q: A guest notices that a glass of Paltrinieri's Radice is slightly cloudy. What explains it?
opts: It referments in bottle and is left on its lees
It is blended with Lambrusco Grasparossa for colour
It is aged for a year in old oak casks
It is a passito made from dried grapes
questions.exp: Radice finishes its fermentation in its own bottle and is never disgorged, so its lees stay in it; it is Sorbara alone, with no Grasparossa and no time in oak.

questions.q: The Paltrinieri family dates its winemaking in the Cristo di Sorbara to which year?
questions.exp: The family dates its bond with Sorbara to 1926 and marked its hundredth year in 2026; 1970 is the year Lambrusco di Sorbara became a DOC of its own.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35; the house's own pages (cantinapaltrinieri.it) were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: 1926 is on the house's own pages and in Primal Wine, Superiore.de and Gambero Rosso; Leclisse is made in tank (a long Charmat in two merchants' words) and without maceration by the house's page, but no source read says it comes from the oldest vines, so that is left out.

The 1970 DOC and its 60 per cent of Sorbara are the Codex's region record, which cites the region's disciplinari; never disgorged rests on Primal Wine and a merchant's sur lie, the single bottling in March and the native yeasts on the house's sheet.

Left out for want of a source: Radice's first vintage, the year the present generation took over (1998 in one account), the founder's dates and calling (a pharmaceutical chemist in one account), so the founder is described as the grandfather and not named.
The house serves Radice at 12 to 13 degrees Celsius on its sheet, warmer than the Codex's 8 to 10 for sparkling wine; the record gives the Codex's figure and says the house suggests a little warmer.

Living names met, none in the fragment's prose save the house's own name: Alberto Paltrinieri and Barbara Galassi, who run the estate, for people.json; a Gambero Rosso address carries his name and is not used.

records.place: Marzeno, Faenza, province of Ravenna, Romagna

wine.name: Scacco Matto
wine.classification: DOCG, raised in 1987 as Albana di Romagna, the first white DOCG in Italy
wine.grapes: Albana alone, picked late from grapes touched by noble rot.
wine.sites: The estate's hill vineyards at Marzeno, a few miles from Faenza in the Romagna hills, on the red, iron rich clays of Marzeno with limestone.
wine.making: Albana is picked late, in several passes through the vineyard, taking only the parts of the bunch and the single berries touched by noble rot. It is fermented in small steel tanks, in some vintages also in used French barriques, and aged in the same vessels for a year and more before bottling, mostly in half bottles.
wine.glass: Deep gold, with candied orange peel, saffron, apricot and acacia honey; rich and sweet yet held up by Albana's firm acidity, with a long, faintly bitter finish of almond.
wine.ageing: Open and honeyed on release, a strong vintage keeps and deepens for many years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius, a little warmer for an older bottle; no need to decant; a small white wine glass.

label.means: Italian for checkmate: the house names its sweet Albanas from chess, Arrocco being castling.
The DOCG for Albana in the Romagna hills, raised in 1987 under the name Albana di Romagna.
A wine of dried or shrivelled grapes; here late picked Albana shrivelled by noble rot.

records.table: Scacco Matto is Fattoria Zerbina's sweet Albana from the hills of Faenza, picked late, berry by berry, where noble rot has shrivelled the grapes. Saffron, apricot honey and candied orange peel ride on firm acidity: pour it cool beside blue cheese or almond pastries.
records.story: Fattoria Zerbina began in 1966, when its founder bought land at Marzeno, a few miles from Faenza in the Romagna hills, and planted its first vines; its first bottle followed in 1970, by the house's account. In 1987 Albana di Romagna became the first white wine in Italy to be raised to DOCG, a promotion widely thought unearned at the time. That same year, as the house tells it, the founder's granddaughter took the estate in hand, set on raising the quality of its Sangiovese and its Albana, and looked to Sauternes for a sweet Albana made from grapes touched by noble rot. In the misty autumn of the Romagna hills the 1987 vintage gave the first Scacco Matto, its name the Italian for checkmate. The house names 1992 as the year its selection of the grapes changed, and in 1995 it first made AR, a riserva of single berries, in only 180 half bottles. Beside the sweet wines it built serious Romagna Sangiovese, Pietramora among it, and Marzieno, a red of Sangiovese with French varieties. For a sommelier Scacco Matto is the bottle that answers those who doubt Albana's DOCG: a sweet wine of noble rot from the Romagna hills, with the acidity to carry its honey.

others.name: AR
others.note: A Romagna Albana Passito Riserva from single berries chosen by hand, first made in 1995 in only 180 half bottles.

others.name: Pietramora
others.note: Romagna Sangiovese, the serious dry red of the estate.

others.name: Marzieno
others.note: A Ravenna IGT red of Sangiovese blended with French varieties: the house's Bordeaux influenced blend.

traps: Albana di Romagna was the first white DOCG of Italy, in 1987, not the first DOCG: red DOCGs such as Barolo and Brunello came before it.
Scacco Matto is a sweet Albana; the house's reds, Pietramora and Marzieno, are Sangiovese led and a separate matter.
The DOCG once named Albana di Romagna was renamed Romagna Albana, so older and newer bottles of Scacco Matto carry different names, and labels also spell it Scaccomatto.

cards.front: Fattoria Zerbina Scacco Matto: which grapes are picked, and how?
cards.back: Late picked Albana, in several passes through the vineyard, taking only the parts of the bunch and single berries touched by noble rot.

cards.front: What happened to Albana di Romagna in 1987, the year of the first Scacco Matto?
cards.back: It became the first white DOCG in Italy.

questions.q: A guest asks what gives Fattoria Zerbina's Scacco Matto its sweetness and its notes of saffron and honey. Which answer is right?
opts: Noble rot on late picked Albana
Sweet grape must added before bottling
Fortification with grape spirit
Grapes frozen on the vine
questions.exp: Scacco Matto is late picked Albana shrivelled by noble rot and chosen in several passes; it is not fortified, and grapes frozen on the vine make an ice wine.

questions.q: Fattoria Zerbina's land at Marzeno near Faenza was bought and first planted in which year?
questions.exp: The founder bought the land and planted in 1966; 1970 brought the first bottle and 1987 the first Scacco Matto.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35; the house's own pages (zerbina.com) were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered: the house's territory page gives 1966 for the founding and 1970 for the first bottle, its Scacco Matto page 1987 for the first vintage, and Vinodabere and Bibenda agree on 1966 and 1987; the label reads Romagna Albana Passito DOCG, Albana di Romagna Passito on older bottles.
Library in tension: p-zerbina leaves founded empty, where the house's own page gives 1966; the record carries 1966 and the library is not changed.
The house's Italian page names used French barriques in some vintages and its English page steel tanks alone; the record keeps the Italian page's fuller account.

Left out on one source: the vintages not made for want of noble rot (Bibenda names 1995, 1999, 2002, 2010 and 2011), some Albana on pergola for more botrytis (Winefriend), the estate's area and the founder's dates and name, so he is described as the grandfather.

One merchant says the DOCG was granted in 1986; the Codex's region record and Bibenda's 1987 stand, and the first white DOCG of Italy is the library's own fact (p-zerbina) and the region record's, so no new source is cited for it.

Living names met, none in the fragment's prose: Cristina Geminiani (Maria Cristina in one account), the founder's granddaughter who runs the estate, and her brother Vincenzo Geminiani, namesake of the founder, for people.json.

records.place: Rivergaro, Val Trebbiola, Colli Piacentini, Emilia

wine.name: Ageno
wine.appellation: Emilia IGT or Vino Bianco, by vintage
wine.grapes: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, in earlier vintages the larger part with Ortrugo and Trebbiano beside it, in later ones alone.
wine.sites: The estate's hill vineyards in the Val Trebbiola near Rivergaro, south of Piacenza, farmed organically; the Malvasia grows in a vineyard the founder himself chose, as the house tells it.
wine.making: Picked by hand and destemmed, the grapes ferment with their own native yeasts and stay long on their skins, as a red would: about a month in earlier vintages and some four months in later ones, in steel or cement. The wine then ages for about a year in large Slavonian oak casks of 40 hectolitres and for two years or more in bottle, and is released when the house judges it ready.
wine.glass: Amber orange, with dried apricot, candied orange peel, black tea and honey; dry and broad, with a firm grip of tannin unusual in a white, fresh acidity and a long, bitter finish.
wine.ageing: Released only when the house judges it ready, and not always in the order of the vintages, it keeps and gains savoury depth for years after.
wine.serve: 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, cooler than a red and warmer than most whites; open it an hour ahead or decant it; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The name of the lawyer who founded La Stoppa in the second half of the nineteenth century.
The regional IGT, the tier below DOC, which many labels of Ageno carry.
White wine with no geographical indication, as the labels of some vintages read.

records.table: Ageno is La Stoppa's skin fermented white from the hills south of Piacenza: Malvasia di Candia left long on its skins and named for the lawyer who founded the estate. Amber, tannic and savoury, it drinks almost like a red, so pour it cool, not cold.
records.story: La Stoppa was founded in the second half of the nineteenth century by a lawyer, the man whose surname the flagship carries, who saw what the Val Trebbiola near Rivergaro could give and began to make wine there. France being then the measure of fine wine, he planted French varieties. In 1973 the Pantaleoni family bought the estate, and in the 1990s the family's daughter took it on. From the middle of that decade the estate turned mainly to the grapes of the Piacenza hills, replanting with Barbera, Bonarda and Malvasia di Candia Aromatica where the French vines had grown, and it came to be farmed organically. In 2002 Ageno was first made: Malvasia fermented on its skins like a red, then aged in large casks and in bottle. The grapes ferment with their own yeasts, and the house releases each vintage only when it judges it ready, so the vintages do not always reach the market in order. Beside Ageno it makes long aged reds of Barbera and Bonarda, Macchiona among them. For a sommelier Ageno shows what a skin fermented white of Emilia can be: a white with the tannin and the patience of a red.

others.name: Macchiona
others.note: Barbera and Bonarda from the vineyard around an old farmhouse of that name, the house's long aged red.

others.name: Trebbiolo
others.note: A younger red of Barbera and Bonarda from the estate.

traps: Ageno is a white wine made like a red: its amber colour and its tannin come from months on the skins.
Ageno is named for the estate's founder, a lawyer of the nineteenth century, not for a village or a vineyard.
Vintages of Ageno are released when the house judges them ready, so an older vintage may reach the list after a younger one.

cards.front: La Stoppa Ageno: what is it made from, and what makes it orange?
cards.back: Malvasia di Candia Aromatica, with some Ortrugo and Trebbiano in earlier vintages, fermented for weeks to months on its skins like a red.

cards.front: Whom is La Stoppa's Ageno named for?
cards.back: The lawyer who founded the estate in the Piacenza hills in the second half of the nineteenth century.

questions.q: A guest is surprised by the grip of tannin in La Stoppa's Ageno, a white. What explains it?
opts: Long fermentation and maceration on the grape skins
Ageing for years in new oak barriques
A share of Barbera in the blend
Noble rot on late picked Malvasia
questions.exp: Ageno stays on its skins for weeks to months, as a red does, and the skins give it tannin; its casks are large ones of 40 hectolitres, not new barriques.

questions.q: What did La Stoppa do with its vineyards from the middle of the 1990s?
opts: Replaced French varieties with Barbera, Bonarda and Malvasia
Planted Pinot Noir and Cabernet Sauvignon for the first time
Sold its vineyards to a cooperative of Piacenza
Turned its whole estate over to Ortrugo
questions.exp: From the mid 1990s the estate turned to the local grapes in place of the French vines its founder had planted in the nineteenth century, so the French vines came first, not last.

report: Searches for this record: 6 of the group's share of 35; the house's own pages (lastoppa.it) were read through search, and no fetch was tried.

The plan's note is answered in part: Rivergaro in the Val Trebbiola is confirmed; the founding is the second half of the nineteenth century on the house's page, so founded is empty; the founder is a lawyer named Ageno, but his first name is Giancarlo on the house's page and Gian Marco in two importers, and no source gives his dates, so he is described and not named.

Plan in tension: the plan's why gives Malvasia with Ortrugo and Trebbiano, as the importers do for earlier vintages (about nine tenths Malvasia), while the house's own Ageno page gives Malvasia di Candia Aromatica alone; the record says both by vintage.

Appellation in tension: retailers list Ageno as Emilia IGT for vintages up to 2020, while one says it moved to Vino Bianco with the 2017 vintage and another lists a 2020 as Vino da Tavola; the record names both and the year of the change is left out.

Maceration: about a month in earlier vintages (Decanter on the 2011, Primal Wine on a 2020) and some four months in later ones (the house's page, Bowler Wine); first made in 2002 by the house's Italian page and a merchant.

Left out for want of a second source: Genoa as the founder's home, the year 1991 for the daughter's start (the house says the mid 1990s), the estate's area, no added sulphur for Ageno in particular, and the vine age.
Some importers call Macchiona the house's flagship red; Ageno is kept as the wine the house is known by abroad, and no swap is proposed.

Living names met, none in the fragment's prose save the family's surname: Elena Pantaleoni, who runs the estate, and Giulio Armani, its cellar master, who also makes wine under his own label, for people.json; her father, who bought the estate in 1973, died before 1991 by Louis Dressner's account.
